The bakery.parent: The Quiet Cost of Frictionless Things

third spaces.parent: Friction is also how we meet

sentences.text: My argument is that every time we remove a small difficulty from daily life we also remove a small piece of competence and a small occasion for meeting other people, and that the sum of these removals is larger than anyone has priced in.
sentences.subject: The Quiet Cost of Frictionless Things

sentences.text: The argument is not against convenience as such.
sentences.subject: The Quiet Cost of Frictionless Things

sentences.text: For eleven years I bought bread from a bakery two streets from my flat, run by a woman named Marta who never remembered my name but always remembered my order.
sentences.subject: The bakery

sentences.text: Everything about the place was inefficient, because she weighed each loaf by hand, chatted with whoever was ahead of me and refused to take cards under five euros.
sentences.subject: The bakery

sentences.text: When the bakery closed, a delivery app took over the street within a month.
sentences.subject: The bakery

sentences.text: The bread I get now arrives in forty minutes, costs less, and comes from a warehouse kitchen that bakes for six neighbourhoods at once.
sentences.subject: The bakery

sentences.text: What I lost was not bread but a fixed point in the week where I was recognised by someone who had no reason to be nice to me.
sentences.subject: The bakery

sentences.text: Skills are built on friction: the resistance of a task is exactly what teaches us how to do it.
sentences.subject: Friction is where skill lives

sentences.text: A navigator who has never been lost does not learn to read a map, and a cook who has never burned a sauce does not learn the temperature of a pan.
sentences.subject: Friction is where skill lives

sentences.text: Researchers who study pilots have found that crews who rely most on automation are the slowest to recover when the automation fails.
sentences.subject: automation

sentences.text: The same researchers note that the skills that decay first are the ones exercised least, which is why the decay is invisible until the day it matters.
sentences.subject: automation

sentences.text: The same pattern shows up in far humbler places, such as the way people who always use a navigation app stop forming mental maps of their own city.
sentences.subject: Friction is where skill lives

sentences.text: Plato worried that writing would weaken memory, and he was partly right.
sentences.subject: Friction is where skill lives

sentences.text: The difference today is the speed and breadth of the removal: we are not outsourcing one skill at a time but dozens at once, and doing it by default rather than by choice. ## Friction is also how we meet
sentences.subject: Friction is where skill lives

sentences.text: Friction is also the medium of civic life, because shared queues, shared counters and shared mistakes are the places where strangers become neighbours.
sentences.subject: Friction is also how we meet

sentences.text: Sociologists call these places third spaces, and they have been closing for decades, long before the apps arrived.
sentences.subject: third spaces

sentences.text: What the apps did was finish the job by making the visit unnecessary.
sentences.subject: Friction is also how we meet

sentences.text: A pharmacy that delivers does not need you to stand in its doorway, and a doorway is where you learn that the man ahead of you is caring for his mother.
sentences.subject: Friction is also how we meet

sentences.text: Each of these encounters is trivial, and that is exactly why nobody defends them when they go.
sentences.subject: third spaces

sentences.text: Yet a city made only of efficient transactions is a city where nobody has a reason to speak to anyone. ## The strongest objection
sentences.subject: third spaces

sentences.text: People who carry shopping up four flights of stairs, or who wait three hours at a clinic, are not grateful for the character it builds, and for many of them frictionless services are a real liberation.
sentences.subject: The strongest objection

sentences.text: I accept this completely, and it changes what I am asking for: I am not asking anyone to suffer, but to notice which difficulties are doing work.
sentences.subject: The strongest objection

sentences.text: Disabled people, carers and the very poor have the strongest claim to convenience, and any defence of friction that ignores them is a defence of privilege.
sentences.subject: The strongest objection

sentences.text: It says that choosing friction deliberately is only a luxury hobby, like baking your own bread, and that a skill kept alive as a pastime is not the same thing as a skill a society depends on.
sentences.subject: pastime

sentences.text: I think this is mostly correct.
sentences.subject: pastime

sentences.text: A pastime keeps one person's hands in practice but it does not keep a shared counter open. ## What to keep
sentences.subject: pastime

sentences.text: The practical conclusion is to treat friction as a resource to be allocated, not as waste to be eliminated, and to ask of each new convenience what it quietly takes away.
sentences.subject: What to keep

sentences.text: A useful test is to ask whether the difficulty teaches something that will be needed when the system fails, and whether it puts people in the same room.
sentences.subject: useful test

sentences.text: Where the answer to both is no, remove the difficulty gladly and without guilt.
sentences.subject: useful test

sentences.text: Where the answer is yes, a service can keep a deliberate, slower option, as some libraries keep a human desk beside the self-checkout.
sentences.subject: useful test

sentences.text: Cities can protect a few counters and queues the way they protect a few parks, because their value is the same kind of value: nobody would build them from scratch for profit, and everybody notices when they are gone.
sentences.subject: counters and queues
